records.place: Thonon-les-Bains, Vin de Savoie Ripaille, on Lake Geneva, Haute-Savoie

wine.name: Ripaille
wine.grapes: Chasselas, the principal grape the appellation sets for the cru of Ripaille and the one the château's white is made from.
wine.sites: The vineyard around the castle on the southern shore of Lake Geneva at Thonon-les-Bains, on gravelly, free draining soil left by the glaciers, its climate softened by the water of the lake.
wine.making: Stainless steel tanks, not barrels, hold its fermentation; it goes through its malolactic fermentation and is bottled with no time in oak, so that nothing stands between the Chasselas and the glass.
wine.glass: Pear, lime and fresh almond over a hint of white blossom, with a soft, slightly chalky texture and a gentle bitter edge of grapefruit pith; dry, light in body and low in acidity, more delicate than sharp.
wine.ageing: For freshness, pour it in its first two or three years; a good year keeps longer and grows softer and nuttier.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, poured straight from the bottle with no decanting; a white wine glass, beside perch from the lake or a Savoie fondue.

label.means: The regional appellation of Savoie, an appellation contrôlée since 1973, which may add the name of a cru.
The cru of the appellation at Thonon-les-Bains, for white wine made chiefly from Chasselas.
The castle of the Dukes of Savoy on Lake Geneva, whose vines surround it.

records.table: Where Amédée VIII of Savoy withdrew in 1434, on the shore of Lake Geneva, Château de Ripaille grows Chasselas on gravelly soil for its white, Ripaille. Light, dry and soft, with pear and almond, open it young and cold.
records.story: Ripaille's first residence, by the château's own account, was built in about 1370 by a Count of Savoy and his wife, on the southern shore of Lake Geneva. In 1434 Amédée VIII (1383 to 1451), Duke of Savoy, withdrew there to a hermitage he had made of his residence, the castle of seven towers, while keeping a hand on his duchy. In 1439 the Council of Basel elected him pope as Felix V; he gave the title up in 1449, and Rome counts him an antipope. A legend of feasting grew up around his retreat, and the French phrase faire ripaille, to feast, is said to come from it. From 1623 Ripaille was a charterhouse of Carthusian monks until the Revolution closed it, and the château traces the tradition of its wine to them. In 1892 a Mulhouse industrialist, the head of the DMC textile mills, bought the ruined estate and restored it, and his granddaughter later created the Fondation Ripaille and gave it the castle. The vines around the castle give the cru of Ripaille its name. Behind its white, Savoie's lakeside Chasselas, light, dry and soft, stand the Dukes of Savoy.

others.name: Comte Rouge
others.note: The estate's red, made from Pinot Noir.

traps: Ripaille is a cru name added to Vin de Savoie, not an appellation of its own, and its white is Chasselas, not the Jacquère of most everyday Savoie whites.
Château de Ripaille gives French Chasselas from the southern shore of Lake Geneva; Fendant, the Valais name for Chasselas, is Swiss.
The tale of feasting at Ripaille is a legend: Amédée VIII went there to live as a hermit, and was later elected pope.

cards.front: Château de Ripaille's white comes from which grape, on what soil, beside which lake?
cards.back: Chasselas, on gravelly, free draining soil beside Lake Geneva, whose water softens the climate.

cards.front: Which Duke of Savoy withdrew to Ripaille in 1434, and what did the Council of Basel make him?
cards.back: Amédée VIII, elected pope as Felix V in 1439; he gave the title up in 1449.

questions.q: Which grape is in the glass when a guest orders the Ripaille of Château de Ripaille?
questions.exp: The cru of Ripaille at Thonon-les-Bains is a white of Chasselas, the lakeside grape; Jacquère is the grape of everyday Savoie whites, and Altesse that of Roussette de Savoie.

questions.q: The Duke of Savoy who withdrew to the castle of Ripaille by Lake Geneva in 1434 was given what title by the Council of Basel in 1439?
questions.exp: The Council of Basel elected Amédée VIII pope as Felix V in 1439; he gave the title up in 1449, and Rome counts him an antipope. He was a duke, never an emperor.

The cahier read through search sets Chasselas as the principal grape of Ripaille with accessory grapes allowed, so the record never says the cru is Chasselas alone; one merchant gives the château's white as Chasselas alone, which the château's own page implies but does not state.
Founded is empty: the château dates its first residence to the 1370s and the castle to 1434, the vines are said to be older, and no source dates a founding of the wine estate.

Left out for want of a second source: full malolactic fermentation and hand picking (one importer), the glacial origin of the gravel (the tourist board only), the main cuvée made as one wine rather than by parcel (the Guide Hachette only), the perlant of the wine (no source), the cru being the château's alone (one wine education site), and the end of the restoration (1900 or 1903 on the château's own pages).
The industrialist of 1892 is described, not named: his dates (1843 to 1918) are in one source only. The Count of Savoy and his wife of the 1370s are described for the same reason.

records.place: Arbin, Vin de Savoie Arbin, in the Combe de Savoie, Savoie

wine.name: Arbin Mondeuse
wine.grapes: Mondeuse Noire alone, as the appellation requires of any red that carries the name Arbin.
wine.sites: The domaine's Mondeuse on the slope of Arbin beneath the Bauges massif, near Montmélian in the Combe de Savoie, on clay and limestone scree that drains freely.
wine.making: Hand picked and destemmed, the Mondeuse was macerated for six to twelve days and raised mainly in stainless steel, with no new oak, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blueberry, blackberry and black cherry over white pepper, violet and a cool stony note, in a deep purple; medium in body, with fresh acidity and firm, slightly rustic tannin.
wine.ageing: In its first few years it is lively and open, though firm of tannin; a strong vintage keeps and softens over a decade or so.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter lets a young bottle open; a large red wine glass, beside diots, the Savoie sausage, or game.

label.means: The regional appellation of Savoie, which may add the name of one of its crus.
The cru on the slope below the Bauges near Montmélian, for reds of Mondeuse Noire alone.
Mondeuse Noire, Savoie's own dark red grape, named on the label beside the cru.

records.table: Savoie's own red grape speaks plainly in Domaine Louis Magnin's Arbin Mondeuse, from clay and limestone scree below the Bauges, destemmed and raised mostly in steel. Blueberry, pepper and violet sit on firm tannin; serve it cool beside a Savoie sausage or charcuterie.
records.story: Near Montmélian, beneath the Bauges massif, the village of Arbin stands on the slope of the Combe de Savoie. Vin de Savoie became an appellation contrôlée by the decree of 4 September 1973, and Arbin is one of the names its label may add, kept for reds of Mondeuse Noire alone. Domaine Louis Magnin was a family domaine of the village, worked by the third generation of its family, with its Mondeuse in Arbin and Roussanne, the Bergeron of Chignin, beside it. The couple who ran it farmed organically and worked some of their parcels by biodynamic methods. Their reds were destemmed, macerated for days rather than weeks and raised mostly in steel, so that the grape's pepper and dark berries show without the gloss of new oak. Beside the Arbin Mondeuse they bottled an old vine Mondeuse and a Chignin-Bergeron called Grand Orgue. In the early 2020s the couple wound the domaine down, and by 2024 the Arbin vines they had leased had passed to Domaine des Ardoisières. To learn Savoie's own red grape, open the Arbin Mondeuse: its bottles keep.

others.name: Arbin Mondeuse Vieilles Vignes
others.note: The domaine's Mondeuse from its old vines at Arbin, bottled apart from the Arbin Mondeuse.

others.name: Chignin-Bergeron Grand Orgue
others.note: Its white of Roussanne, the grape Savoie calls Bergeron at Chignin.

traps: Arbin on a Savoie label means Mondeuse Noire alone; Mondeuse Blanche is a different, white grape, the one DNA work names as a parent of Syrah.
Domaine Louis Magnin was wound down in the early 2020s, and by 2024 its leased Arbin vines had passed to Domaine des Ardoisières, so later Mondeuse from them carries that estate's name.
Chignin-Bergeron, the domaine's white, is Roussanne; plain Chignin is chiefly Jacquère.

report: Swap proposed: the domaine has closed. Two merchants (iDealwine and Les Caves de Pyrène) and a forum report 2022 as the couple's last vintage, and iDealwine and an importer of the Ardoisières report that its leased Arbin vines passed to Domaine des Ardoisières (2024 by iDealwine, 2022 by the importer). A house that no longer makes wine teaches history, not a cellar, and it overlaps the Ardoisières pick; a candidate that keeps the Arbin Mondeuse lesson is Domaine des Fils de Charles Trosset of Arbin (Mondeuse, its founder dead in 2000 by one importer), or Domaine Fabien Trosset of Arbin (taken on in 2011), to be confirmed by the refuter; the record as written stays true either way.

The cuvée is named Arbin Mondeuse on the importer's page; the domaine also bottled Arbin Mondeuse La Rouge, Tout un Monde, Vieilles Vignes and La Brova, and the making given is the plain Arbin Mondeuse's (the importer: destemmed, maceration of up to twelve days, mostly steel with a small part in older barrels; iDealwine: destemmed, six days in steel).
Founded is empty: the domaine is the third generation of its family by two merchants, and no source gives a year.

Left out for want of agreement or a second source: the years of the organic and biodynamic work (2007 and 2009 by one merchant, 2010 and 2012 by another, 2007 for one parcel by the importer), the length of the élevage (a year by one, eighteen months for the Vieilles Vignes by another), the punching down in the first days (the importer only), and the year the vines passed to the Ardoisières.
Les Caves de Pyrène is read and not listed: its pages carry a living writer's name in the address.
Living names for people.json, for the merge agent: the couple who ran the domaine, named on every merchant's page; they are never named here, the house keeping its name.

records.place: Cevins, in the Tarentaise valley, IGP Vin des Allobroges, Savoie

wine.name: Quartz
wine.grapes: Altesse alone, the grape of Roussette de Savoie.
wine.sites: The terraces of the slope of Cevins in the Tarentaise, as steep as sixty per cent, on poor, stony soil over schist.
wine.making: Raised in oak barrels for a year or more before it is bottled, by the merchants' sheets, which differ on the length; the terraces are worked by hand and farmed by biodynamic methods.
wine.glass: Quince, white peach and bergamot over a smoky, flinty edge, with a touch of honey and toasted almond; dry, taut and long, with bright acidity and a fine, stony grip.
wine.ageing: Tight when young, it opens after three or four years and keeps for a decade or more, gaining honey and hazelnut as Altesse does.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The protected geographical indication of the Savoie departments, under which the domaine bottles its wines.
The village of the Tarentaise whose terraced slope of schist gives the wine.
The cuvée's name, a mineral: the domaine names its wines for rocks and minerals.

records.table: Quartz, Domaine des Ardoisières' Altesse, comes from the schist terraces of Cevins in the Tarentaise, abandoned until the replanting of 1998, and is raised in barrel and bottled as IGP Vin des Allobroges. Taut and smoky, with quince and bergamot, it opens with an hour of air.
records.story: Vines grew on the slope of Cevins, in the Tarentaise valley of Savoie, from Roman times, by the accounts of those who replanted it, but its stone terraces were later overgrown and abandoned. In 1997 the mayor of Cevins set out to bring the vineyard back, and in 1998 the replanting began, led by an experienced Savoie grower, as the old terraces were cleared and rebuilt. The slope is as steep as sixty per cent and its soil a poor, stony schist, and it is farmed by biodynamic methods. The domaine's wines were bottled as IGP Vin des Allobroges, not under the Savoie appellation, and given the names of rocks, soils and minerals, Quartz and Argile among them. A younger grower joined the founder in the 2000s and later took the domaine on alone. The Arbin vines leased by Domaine Louis Magnin came to the domaine in the early 2020s, when the couple behind that house retired. From a slope that was lost and won back, Quartz gives Altesse grown on schist.

others.name: Argile Blanc
others.note: The domaine's white named for clay, also bottled as IGP Vin des Allobroges.

traps: Quartz is IGP Vin des Allobroges, never Roussette de Savoie, though it is made of Altesse, the grape of Roussette.
The domaine's cuvée names are rocks, soils and minerals, not places: Quartz and Argile are wines, and Cevins is the village of the terraces.

cards.front: Quartz, the white of Domaine des Ardoisières, is made of what grape, grown where?
cards.back: Altesse alone, from the replanted terraces of schist at Cevins in the Tarentaise.

cards.front: When did the replanting of the abandoned Cevins terraces, the birth of Domaine des Ardoisières, begin?

questions.q: The label of Domaine des Ardoisières' Quartz says IGP Vin des Allobroges. What grape made it?
questions.exp: Quartz is Altesse alone from the Cevins terraces, the grape of Roussette de Savoie, though it carries the IGP; Jacquère is the everyday Savoie white.

questions.q: Which village of the Tarentaise saw vines go back onto its abandoned slope in 1998, the start of Domaine des Ardoisières?
questions.exp: The domaine replanted the schist terraces of Cevins in the Tarentaise; Arbin, Jongieux and Chignin are crus of the Savoie appellation.

report: No primary source: the domaine's own site did not come up in any search, so every fact rests on two of the merchants and importers listed; no house page was read.
Founded is 1998, the year of the first planting (May 1998, Altesse) in most accounts; one merchant gives 1997, the year the mayor of Cevins launched the project, and the story gives both.

Why the wines are IGP rather than Savoie rests on a writer's own site and a guide quoted by a merchant (the slope left outside the appellation, partly for want of sun), so the record says only that they are bottled as IGP and never why.

Left out for want of agreement: the year the younger grower joined (2003 or 2005), the year he took over alone (2010 or 2014), the year the Magnin vines passed to the domaine (2022 or 2024), the share of new oak and the length of the élevage for Quartz (twelve months with a quarter new, a year in barrels of three to five years, eighteen months in one vintage), and fermentation in barrel with native yeasts (one merchant).

Left out for want of a second source: phylloxera as the cause of the slope's ruin, the slope's south south east aspect, loam and sand among the schist, the schist's contrast with the limestone of most of Savoie, the month of the first planting (May 1998) and Altesse as its first grape, the rebuilt dry stone walls, the founder's earlier estate at Fréterive, an outside investor who saved the project, and the cuvées Schiste and Améthyste (Persan with Mondeuse).
Living names for people.json, for the merge agent: the founder, the grower who took the domaine on, and the mayor of Cevins of 1997, all named in the merchants' pages; none is named here.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35.

records.place: Aimavigne in Jongieux, west of the Lac du Bourget, Savoie

wine.name: Roussette de Savoie Marestel
wine.grapes: Altesse alone, as Roussette de Savoie requires.
wine.sites: The Marestel slope above Jongieux and Lucey at the foot of the Mont du Chat, where Altesse was first grown on terraces; the family's cellar stands below it in the hamlet of Aimavigne.
wine.making: After fermentation the Altesse is raised for at least a year in large oak foudres rather than small barrels, the house's chosen way with it, and the family holds its wines back in bottle before they leave the cellar.
wine.glass: Quince, bergamot and white peach over honey, almond and a smoky note, turning with age towards beeswax and dried apricot; full, and dry or close to it, lively in acidity, its finish firm and lasting.
wine.ageing: Five years or so pass before it opens, and a strong year then carries it for decades.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; a young bottle is the better for being decanted an hour ahead; a large white wine glass, beside lake fish in a cream sauce or a Beaufort.

label.means: The appellation for whites of Altesse alone, named for the russet tinge of the ripe grapes.
One of the four crus whose name may follow Roussette de Savoie, the slope above Jongieux and Lucey.
The grape of Roussette, attested in Savoie since the fourteenth century.

records.table: Patience is the house's way at Domaine Dupasquier: its Roussette de Savoie Marestel, Altesse from the terraced slope above Jongieux, is raised in large oak foudres and held back in bottle. Quince, bergamot and honey on a firm, lively spine, it repays years in the cellar.
records.story: The Marestel slope climbs above Jongieux and Lucey, at the foot of the Mont du Chat and west of the Lac du Bourget. By the appellation's account it takes its name from a counsellor of the Duke of Savoy ennobled in 1563, and its vines were first grown on terraces whose wine was kept for the tables of princes. Altesse, the grape of Roussette, is attested in Savoie from the fourteenth century. Roussette de Savoie was first recognised in 1957 and confirmed as an appellation contrôlée in 1973, and Marestel is one of four crus whose name may follow it, with Frangy, Monterminod and Monthoux. The Dupasquier family has grown vines in the hamlet of Aimavigne, at the foot of the Marestel hill, for five generations by the accounts of a merchant and a wine guide. The house is known for patience: its Altesse is raised in large oak foudres, and the family holds its wines back in bottle before they are sold. Its Marestel shows what time makes of Altesse: the quince and bergamot of youth turn towards honey and beeswax over the years.

others.name: Roussette de Savoie Altesse
others.note: The house's Roussette de Savoie without the cru name, of Altesse like the Marestel.

traps: Marestel is a cru of Roussette de Savoie, so it is Altesse alone; Jongieux on a Vin de Savoie label is a separate cru of the same village, which also gives reds.
Roussette is the appellation and Altesse the grape: a guest who asks for a Roussette de Savoie is asking for Altesse.

cards.front: Name the appellation, the grape and the village of Domaine Dupasquier's Marestel.
cards.back: Roussette de Savoie Marestel, Altesse alone, from the slope above Jongieux at the foot of the Mont du Chat.

cards.front: By the appellation's account, where does the name of Marestel, Dupasquier's cru, come from?
cards.back: From a counsellor of the Duke of Savoy ennobled in 1563, whose name the terraced slope took.

questions.q: In what does Domaine Dupasquier raise its Roussette de Savoie Marestel?
opts: Two years in new small barrels
Under a veil of yeast in old barrels
On its skins for weeks in clay jars
questions.exp: The house raises its Altesse in large oak foudres and holds it back in bottle; the veil of yeast is the Jura's way with vin jaune, not Savoie's with Altesse.

questions.q: The counsellor of the Duke of Savoy whose name the Marestel slope took was ennobled, by the appellation's account, in which year?
questions.exp: The appellation traces Marestel to a counsellor ennobled in 1563; 1973 is the year Roussette de Savoie was confirmed as an appellation contrôlée.

report: The appellation's history (the name from a counsellor of the Duke of Savoy ennobled in 1563, the terraces, the tables of princes, Altesse in the fourteenth century, 1957 and 1973, the four crus) is the INAO's own, read through search; the INAO names the counsellor and the duke, and they are described here because no second source gave their dates.
The generations are five by a merchant and the wine guide listed and four by an older forum post, so the story says five by those accounts.

The late release: one merchant gives close to a year in foudre and a year in bottle before release for the Marestel, and the guide says the family keeps mature vintages; the record says only that the family holds its wines back in bottle, and gives no length.
Founded is empty: no source gives a year for the domaine.

Left out for want of a second source: the slope's gradient and south west aspect (up to 65 per cent by one merchant), the age the Marestel can reach (thirty to forty years by one merchant), and the farming without synthetic products (one guide).
Note for the voice editor: the wine guide's name carries two surnames, as Louis/Dressner's does in the Jura group; it is the publisher's name, not an author's byline.

Living names for people.json, for the merge agent: the couple who run the domaine, the fifth generation, named in the merchants' pages; neither is named here. A different house, Domaine Dupasquier et Fils of Nuits-Saint-Georges in Burgundy, appears in the Guide Hachette, and it is not this one.
Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 35.

records.place: Mérignat, Bugey Cerdon, in the Ain, Bugey

wine.name: Bugey Cerdon
wine.grapes: Gamay for the larger part, about seven parts in ten or more, with Poulsard for the rest; the share moves from year to year.
wine.sites: The family's vines of Gamay and Poulsard around Mérignat, one of the villages of the Ain where the name Cerdon may be used.
wine.making: Pressed, the juice ferments slowly with its own yeasts in tanks cooled to hold the fermentation back, until part of its sugar has become alcohol. It is then lightly filtered and bottled with its remaining sugar and yeast, with no liqueur de tirage, so the fermentation ends in the bottle.
wine.glass: Wild strawberry, raspberry and redcurrant over pink grapefruit and a touch of rose, in a pale cherry pink; gently sweet and softly foaming, fresh and light in body.
wine.ageing: Within a year or so of release, before its fruit and its sparkle fade, is the time to open it.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass or a tulip, with a fruit tart, a praline tart or as an aperitif.

label.means: The Bugey appellation with the name Cerdon, kept for sparkling rosé of Gamay and Poulsard.
A single fermentation, begun in tank and finished in the bottle, with no sugar or yeast added.

records.table: Domaine Renardat-Fâche's Bugey Cerdon owes its sweetness and its foam to one fermentation, begun in tank and finished in the bottle with nothing added: a pink sparkling wine of Gamay and Poulsard from the Ain. Low in alcohol and full of wild strawberry, it meets dessert cold.
records.story: Between the Jura and Savoie, in the Ain, the Bugey village of Cerdon gives its name to a pink sparkling wine made around it by the ancestral method: one fermentation, begun in the vat and finished in the bottle, with no sugar or yeast added. The Renardat family of Mérignat, one of the villages of the Cerdon area, has grown vines for generations, by its own account more than eight. After the Second World War, the family says, an earlier generation worked out with a few other growers the way of making Cerdon by the méthode ancestrale. The father of the present grower returned to the domaine in 1974 and later installed its first insulated tanks, which let the fermentation be slowed and held by cold, and his son joined him in 1996. From 2008 the family converted its vines to organic farming. In 2009 the Bugey became an appellation contrôlée, with Cerdon one of its named wines, kept for sparkling rosé of Gamay and Poulsard. The house's Cerdon is a blend of the two whose share moves with the year. Every bubble and every trace of sweetness in it comes from the grape alone.

others.name: Au Commencement
others.note: A second sparkling rosé of Gamay and Poulsard in the house's range, sold under its own cuvée name.

traps: Cerdon is not made by the traditional method of Champagne: there is one fermentation only, finished in the bottle, and no liqueur de tirage.
Bugey Cerdon is an appellation of the Ain, not a cru of Vin de Savoie, and a wine labelled Cerdon is always pink and sparkling.
Poulsard, Cerdon's second grape, is the Jura's red, the grape called Ploussard at Pupillin.

cards.front: Which grapes and which method make Domaine Renardat-Fâche's Bugey Cerdon?
cards.back: Gamay and Poulsard, by the méthode ancestrale: one fermentation, begun in tank and finished in the bottle, nothing added.

cards.front: What did the present grower's father bring to Renardat-Fâche after his return in 1974?
cards.back: Its first insulated tanks, which let the fermentation be slowed and held by cold.

questions.q: Where do the sweetness and the bubbles of Renardat-Fâche's Bugey Cerdon come from?
opts: One fermentation finished in the bottle, nothing added
A second fermentation with added sugar and yeast
Carbon dioxide pumped into a sweetened rosé
A sweet dosage added after the disgorging
questions.exp: Cerdon's single fermentation, slowed by cold and finished in the bottle, keeps the grape's own sugar and gas; sugar and yeast added for a second fermentation is the traditional method of Champagne.

questions.q: In 2009 a region of the Ain became an appellation contrôlée, with Cerdon one of its named wines. Which region is it?
questions.exp: The Bugey became an appellation contrôlée by the decree of 20 October 2009, Cerdon among its named wines; Savoie and the Jura have their own appellations.

report: The house's own pages, read through search, give its dates: the family's work on the ancestral method after the Second World War, the father's return in 1974 and his insulated tanks, the son's arrival in 1996 and the organic conversion from 2008; the INAO gives the appellation of 2009 and the Cerdon rules (Gamay and Poulsard alone, rosé, no liqueur de tirage).

The blend moves: the house's page gives about seven parts Gamay to three of Poulsard and the importer's sheet for 2023 about four to one, so the record says about two thirds or more and that the share moves.
The generations disagree: more than eight by the house, seventh by one importer and sixth by the son in another's interview, so the story gives the house's figure as its own account.
The couple of the post war years are named on the house's page; no source gave their dates, so they are an earlier generation of the family here.

Left out for want of a second source: the Bugey's recognition as a VDQS in 1958 (the house's page alone, not its own fact), the biodynamic certification from the 2022 vintage (one importer), the father's long supply of a famous restaurant of the Dombes (one importer), and the alcohol of the finished wine (8 per cent on the house's pages, 7.5 on the importer's sheet).

Living names for people.json, for the merge agent: the father and the son who run the domaine, and a member of the family who wrote an importer's harvest report of 2011; none is named here, the house keeping its name.
No Codex record in tension: the Codex's own question on Bugey gives 2009, Gamay leading and Poulsard beside it, as here.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35.

changed: wine.grapes: "about two thirds or more,"; now "about seven parts in ten or more,": The house's page gives about seven parts Gamay to three of Poulsard and the importer's sheet for 2023 about four to one, so seven in ten or more is the honest floor; two thirds was looser than either.

wine.making: "Picked by hand and pressed, the juice ferments slowly in cold steel tanks with its own yeasts until it reaches about six degrees of alcohol. It is ..."; now "Pressed, the juice ferments slowly with its own yeasts in tanks cooled to hold the fermentation back, until part of its sugar has become alcohol. ...": The house's page gives the partial fermentation in cooled tanks with the grapes' own yeasts, the light filtration and the bottling, and the INAO the fermentation stopped by cold and resumed in the bottle. Hand picking, about six degrees in tank, steel, the cold cellar and the emptying of the bottles into a tank to filter and rebottle rest on one source or none and go.

others.0.note: "A Vin de France sparkling wine by the ancestral method, bottled on its lees, outside the appellation."; now "A second sparkling rosé of Gamay and Poulsard in the house's range, sold under its own cuvée name.": The house's shop lists Au Commencement and a product listing gives it as a sparkling rosé of Gamay and Poulsard; that it is a Vin de France bottled on its lees was in no source read.
